planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring directly into shallow, rocky, highly alkaline limestone soil in full sun; this pine rockland endemic is frost-tender and suited only to Zone 10-11 South Florida landscapes.

directions: Pineland Golden Trumpet is a low, woody-based scrambling subshrub endemic to the limestone pine rocklands and adjacent rocky glades of Miami-Dade County and the Florida Keys, where it is one of the characteristic understory wildflowers growing in full sun between slash pines. Bright yellow, funnel-shaped flowers open nearly continuously through the warm months atop wiry stems clothed in small, leathery, oval leaves, and the plant exudes a milky sap typical of the dogbane family. In the garden it performs best as a sprawling groundcover or trailing edge plant in shallow, rocky, highly alkaline limestone soil with sharp drainage, requiring almost no irrigation once established. Light pruning after a flush of bloom keeps the mounding habit tidy, and plants are best sourced as container stock from South Florida native-plant specialty growers rather than attempted from seed.

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring at the base of a trellis, fence, or shrub in rocky, well-drained limestone soil in full sun; frost-tender and suited only to Zone 10-11 South Florida pine rockland and hammock-edge gardens.

directions: Skyblue Clustervine is a slender, twining perennial vine of the morning glory family native to the margins of pine rocklands and tropical hardwood hammocks in Miami-Dade County and the Florida Keys, where it threads through low shrubs and fence lines in full sun. Clusters of small, funnel-shaped, true sky-blue flowers open through a long warm-season bloom period, drawing bees and other pollinators to an otherwise subtle vine. It thrives in thin, rocky, well-drained limestone soil and tolerates drought and salt-tinged air once established, making it well suited to trellises, split-rail fencing, or a mailbox post in a South Florida native garden. Cut back old growth in late winter to refresh the vine before its main spring and summer flowering push.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring into thin, rocky, alkaline limestone soil beneath an open pine canopy or in full sun; frost-tender and suited only to Zone 10-11 South Florida pine rockland landscapes.

directions: Quailberry is a low, wiry, holly-leaved subshrub that forms loose mats across the exposed limestone of Miami-Dade pine rocklands, its small spiny-toothed leaves echoing a miniature holly. Inconspicuous flowers give way to bright red, long-lasting berries held close to the stems, providing color and a food source for ground-feeding birds through much of the year. Adapted to grow directly in thin, rocky, highly alkaline pine rockland soil under the dappled light of an open pine canopy, it is extremely drought-tolerant once rooted in and needs no supplemental fertilizer. Use it as a textured, low-maintenance groundcover along pathway edges or beneath taller native shrubs in a South Florida native or xeriscape planting.
